title: Timeline Board
context: Grade 4, and where the chapter drops a.m. and p.m. for four digits. An adult sees a rule, add twelve in the afternoon, which works for most of the day. What is actually being settled is what the four digits count: the hours and minutes since midnight. Read that way, the two twelve o'clock hours stop being exceptions. 12 noon is twelve hours after midnight, 1200 hours, and a time just after midnight has had no whole hour yet, so it starts with 00. The page's notes add twelve only to times from one o'clock in the afternoon on, and show no time in the hour after noon or after midnight. Its exercise tests noon and midnight, so the timeline is what teaches them.

writeup.why: Write a time as four digits counted from midnight, with the twelve o'clock hours right, and change a 24-hour time back to a.m. or p.m.
writeup.look: The page's timeline drawn large, nought to twenty-four hours above the 12-hour times, a marker with two readouts, and a departure board beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Timeline Board' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the times written against the times this phase holds, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each time settles and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The timeline runs across the top of the working area, a bar 1056 by 64 at 80,262, numbered nought to twenty-four in ink along its top edge, one hour to every 44, with the noon post at 608. From the left-hand midnight post to the noon post the bar is sky blue, and from the noon post to the right-hand midnight post it is amber. Under the bar, from 336, the 12-hour times are written at their hours: 12 midnight, 1 a.m. to 11 a.m., 12 noon, 1 p.m. to 11 p.m., and 12 midnight again, with a moon over each midnight post and a sun over the noon post. The marker is a near-black pin that slides along the bar a minute at a time, and two readout tags hang under it and ride with it, stopping at the working area's edge near either end: the 12-hour readout, a time with a.m. or p.m., and under it the four-digit readout, its two hour digits in vermilion and its two minute digits in deep blue, followed by the word hours. The add twelve gate stands on the bar at the one o'clock mark of the afternoon, at 652. When the marker reaches it the gate swings open and a small tag reading add twelve rides with the marker for the rest of the afternoon and evening; in the hour from 12 noon to one the gate stays shut. The right-hand midnight post reads 0000 hours for the start of the next day, and a small card beside it says the page also writes 2400 hours, a name for midnight at the end of a day. The clock bay stands at the lower left, 560 by 216 at 80,500: two clock faces, each 180 across, a true clock and a clock that gains or loses a set number of minutes every hour, with the minutes gained or lost so far written between them. The departure board stands at the lower right, 470 by 170 at 670,500, as rows of times to change, each row with a blank for its twin. The take twelve control lies under it, 470 by 50 at 670,680: it takes twelve from an hour of thirteen to twenty-three and stays unlit for an hour of twelve or less. A pale pin can stand on the bar beside the marker to show where a child's answer would be. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve keys three across, the ten digits, a colon and a clear key, with keys reading a.m., p.m. and hours over it. The answer slot takes either a 12-hour time with its label box or four digits and the word hours, whichever the question asks for, and a four-digit answer has all four places drawn, so the nought before a one-digit hour is seen as a place to fill. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The hour hand, every hour tile and hour cell, the hours column, and the hours of a time the stage splits into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand, every minute tile and minute cell, the minutes column and the minutes of a split time are deep blue. The second hand, every second cell and the seconds column are reddish purple. The a.m. half of the day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on a track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every clock rim, minute mark, clock number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket, guide line and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined, before any of them is told by a colour. A figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. The four digits on this stage count the hours and minutes since the left-hand midnight post, so 12 noon reads 1200 hours with the gate shut, and every time between that post and one o'clock in the morning begins with two noughts. The marker's readout does not show 2400 hours: that name for midnight at the end of a day is on the card beside the right-hand post, and the post itself reads 0000 hours for the start of the next day.
writeup.finish: The card shows the timeline with every time the child changed marked on it, each with its 12-hour and its 24-hour name.

phases.win: each morning time is written in four digits with the word hours, and none of them carries a.m.
phases.does: slides the marker through the morning, reading each time in four digits and filling a nought before a one-digit hour
phases.goal: the 24-hour clock counts from midnight and writes four digits, two for the hours and two for the minutes, with a nought filling a one-digit hour
phases.says: Read the four digits. Which two are the hours, and which two are the minutes?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write 8:05 a.m. as four digits. Which two digits are the hours?
phases.feels: the four digits count the whole day from midnight, so a morning time and an evening time never share a number
phases.hands: Read a real bus or train timetable in 24-hour time with the class. Pick three morning departures, cover their first two digits, and ask what the last two tell. Then write 6:40 a.m. and 10:15 a.m. on the board and have the class write them as four digits.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many digits does a 24-hour time have? Second rung, the phase's: which two are the hours, and which two the minutes? Third rung: the marker is set on an o'clock time in the morning, and the child writes its four digits before the minutes come back. The pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: seven is one digit, and a nought in front of a number does not usually get written.
wrong.move: writes 705 hours for 7:05 a.m., with three digits.
wrong.screen: the four-digit readout under the marker shows all four places drawn, 0705, and its first place, the nought, lights in vermilion as part of the hours. The child's 705 is laid under it place by place from the left, so its hours would read seventy and its last place stands empty. The child's answer stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: since a.m. and p.m. were met, times of day have been written with a label after them, and leaving it off feels like leaving the answer unfinished.
wrong.move: writes 0705 a.m., keeping the label on a four-digit time.
wrong.screen: the marker is slid on to seven in the evening, and the four-digit readout changes to 1905 hours while the 12-hour readout reads 7:05 p.m. It is slid back, and the readout returns to 0705 hours. Each set of four digits names one moment of the day, so the label has nothing left to say, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the timeline with the marker at a morning time and both readouts showing
phases.soWhat: The 24-hour clock writes four digits, two for the hours and two for the minutes, with no a.m. or p.m.
phases.concept: Four digits, no a.m. or p.m.

phases.win: the hour digits jump by twelve as the marker passes into each hour, and the four digits settle
phases.does: moves the marker through the afternoon and evening, adding twelve to each hour and writing the four digits
phases.goal: from one o'clock in the afternoon to just before midnight, twelve is added to the hour
phases.says: Past one in the afternoon, add twelve to the hour. What do you get?
phases.check: Write 7:50 p.m. and 2:05 p.m. in 24-hour time.
phases.feels: the hours keep counting past twelve, so an afternoon hour is twelve more than its 12-hour name
phases.hands: Draw the timeline on the board, nought to twenty-four above and the 12-hour times below. Point at one o'clock in the afternoon and ask how many hours have passed since midnight. Then do four o'clock and eight o'clock in the evening, and let the class find the rule for themselves: twelve more than the 12-hour hour.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is the time before noon or after it? Second rung, the phase's: is it one o'clock in the afternoon or later, and what is twelve more than its hour? Third rung: the marker is set on one o'clock in the afternoon exactly, and the child writes its four digits before the later time comes back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: the morning hours kept their numbers in the first phase, and nothing in the figures 9:25 says evening.
wrong.move: writes 0925 hours for 9:25 p.m., as if afternoon and evening hours kept their numbers the way morning hours do.
wrong.screen: the marker is slid to 9:25 p.m., far along the amber part of the bar, and the four-digit readout reads 2125 hours with the add twelve tag riding beside it. A pale pin shows the child's 0925 in the sky blue part, at 9:25 a.m., and both stay on the bar with the child's answer in the slot.

wrong.why: twelve has to be added somewhere, and the minutes are the last digits written.
wrong.move: adds twelve to the minutes instead of the hour, and writes 0937 hours for 9:25 p.m.
wrong.screen: the marker crosses the gate, and the minute digits under it stay at 25 while the hour digits jump by twelve, from nine to twenty-one. A pale pin shows where 0937 hours stands, in the morning, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside the readout's 2125.

wrong.why: the true time is the one found by counting on, and the clock that is wrong seems to have no answer of its own.
wrong.move: gives the true time, 1320 hours, when the question asks what a clock that gains three minutes an hour shows four hours after it is set right at 9:20 a.m.
wrong.screen: the clock bay runs both clocks from 9:20 a.m. for four hours at walking pace, and each hour the gaining clock's minute hand runs three marks further ahead, three, six, nine and twelve minutes in all. The true clock stops at 1:20 p.m. and the gaining clock at 1:32 p.m., and the marker slides to the gaining clock's time, reading 1332 hours. The child's 1320 stays in the slot beside it.

phases.screen: the marker just past one o'clock in the afternoon, with the add twelve gate open
phases.soWhat: From one o'clock in the afternoon to just before midnight, twelve is added to the hour.

phases.win: noon reads 1200 hours with the gate shut, and the time just after midnight begins with two noughts
phases.does: sets the marker on noon and just after it, then just after midnight, and tries the gate each time
phases.goal: 12 noon is 1200 hours with nothing added, and a time just after midnight starts with 00
phases.says: Is twelve noon twelve hours after midnight, or twenty-four? How many whole hours have passed just after midnight?
phases.check: Write 12:50 p.m. and 12:50 a.m. in 24-hour time. How many whole hours have passed since midnight at each?
phases.feels: the digits count from the midnight post, so noon is twelve hours along and just after midnight no hour has passed
phases.hands: On the board timeline, point at 12 noon and ask how many hours have passed since midnight. Then point just after midnight, at ten past twelve at night, and ask the same. Write 1200 hours and 0010 hours under them, and ask why neither has had twelve added.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is the time just after noon, or just after midnight? Second rung, the phase's: how many whole hours have passed since midnight? Third rung: the marker is set on the noon post itself, and the child writes 1200 hours before the minutes after it come back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: the page's notes add twelve in the afternoon, and noon looks like the first time of the afternoon.
wrong.move: adds twelve to 12 noon, as for the afternoon hours, and writes 2400 hours, which names midnight at the end of a day.
wrong.screen: the marker stands on the noon post with the gate shut, and the four-digit readout reads 1200 hours: twelve hours have passed since the left-hand midnight post, and the twelve on the bar above the post says so. A pale pin shows where the child's number belongs, on the right-hand post, whose card names 2400 hours as midnight at the end of a day. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: 12:35 p.m. carries p.m., and every p.m. time in the page's notes gained twelve.
wrong.move: adds twelve to 12:35 p.m. and writes 2435 hours.
wrong.screen: the marker stands thirty-five minutes past the noon post, short of the gate, which stays shut, and the readout reads 1235 hours. The bar ends at twenty-four, at the right-hand midnight post, and no place on it reads 2435; the child's number is written small past the end of the bar, and it stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the 12-hour name starts with twelve, and a morning hour keeps its number.
wrong.move: writes 1235 hours for 12:35 a.m., keeping the twelve of its 12-hour name.
wrong.screen: the marker is slid to 12:35 a.m., thirty-five minutes after the left-hand midnight post, and the readout reads 0035 hours: no whole hour has passed since midnight, so the hour places hold two noughts. A pale pin shows the child's 1235 hours thirty-five minutes past the noon post, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the page gives midnight the name 2400 hours without saying it is for the end of a day, and thirty-five minutes on from it looks like 2435.
wrong.move: writes 2435 hours for 12:35 a.m., counting on from 2400 hours, the name for midnight at the end of a day.
wrong.screen: the marker stands thirty-five minutes after the left-hand midnight post, and the readout reads 0035 hours. The card by the right-hand post is lit, naming 2400 hours as midnight at the end of a day, and the post itself reads 0000 hours, where the new day starts again. The child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the marker on the noon post with the add twelve gate shut, and the left-hand midnight post lit
phases.soWhat: 12 noon is 1200 hours, and a time just after midnight begins with 00.

phases.win: each board time gets its 12-hour twin with a.m. or p.m., and the marker lands on both at once
phases.does: reads each board time, takes twelve from an hour of thirteen to twenty-three, and writes the 12-hour time with a.m. or p.m.
phases.goal: an hour of 13 to 23 has twelve taken away and is p.m., minutes past 00 are twelve a.m., and minutes past 12 stay twelve p.m.
phases.says: Is the hour more than twelve? Then take twelve away and write p.m.
phases.check: Change 1415 hours, 0915 hours and 0015 hours into 12-hour times.
phases.feels: the take twelve control lights from one o'clock in the afternoon on, the same place the gate opened
phases.hands: Write five departures from a 24-hour timetable on cards, one of them in the hour after noon and one in the hour after midnight. Groups change each into a 12-hour time with a.m. or p.m., and stand the cards along the board timeline to check.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is the hour more than twelve, twelve itself, or less? Second rung, the phase's: what does taking twelve away leave? Third rung: the board is cut to one time with an hour of thirteen to twenty-three, and the child takes twelve from it before the other rows come back. The pad and the label keys stay open.

wrong.why: the one in front looks like the part that makes the hour big, and dropping it is quicker than taking away.
wrong.move: drops the first digit of 16 and writes 6:50 p.m. for 1650 hours, instead of taking twelve away.
wrong.screen: the take twelve control lights under the board row, and sixteen less twelve is written in vermilion: four. The marker slides to 1650 hours on the bar and its 12-hour readout reads 4:50 p.m., and a pale pin shows the child's 6:50 p.m. two hours further along. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: taking twelve away is the rule just learnt for the afternoon hours, and an hour of twelve looks like one more of them.
wrong.move: takes twelve from 1219 hours and writes 0:19 p.m.
wrong.screen: the take twelve control stays unlit for an hour of twelve, and the marker slides to nineteen minutes past the noon post, where the 12-hour readout reads 12:19 p.m. No hour on the 12-hour row under the bar is called nought, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the four digits begin with noughts, and copying the hour digits is what worked for the other morning times.
wrong.move: writes 0:26 a.m. for 0026 hours, copying the two noughts as the hour.
wrong.screen: the marker slides to twenty-six minutes after the left-hand midnight post, and the 12-hour readout reads 12:26 a.m. The 12-hour row under the bar starts at 12 midnight and goes on to 1 a.m., so the hour just after midnight is called twelve. The child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the departure board of 24-hour times, with the take twelve control beside it
phases.soWhat: To change back, take twelve from an hour of thirteen to twenty-three and write p.m. An hour of 12 keeps its twelve, and 0026 hours is 12:26 a.m.

writeup.delight: The second phase, when the marker is swept slowly from the late morning into the afternoon. The four-digit readout climbs in even steps, 1158, 1159, 1200, and on through 1259 to 1300 without a jump, while the 12-hour readout climbs to 12:59 p.m. and then drops back to 1:00 p.m. At that moment the gate swings open and its add twelve tag slides under the marker, carrying exactly the twelve hours the 12-hour readout set aside when it began again from one. It can be swept back and forth as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the marker stands at a morning time with both readouts showing under it. On the second the marker stands just past one o'clock in the afternoon with the add twelve gate open beside it. On the third the marker stands on the noon post with the gate shut, and the left-hand midnight post is lit. On the fourth the departure board is filled with 24-hour times and the take twelve control waits under it, unlit. The running count at the top left holds the times written against the times this phase holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the marker, or the gate, or the noon post, or the top row of the board, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many hours have passed since midnight. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: The whole timeline with both readouts, the add twelve gate, the departure board, the take twelve control and the clock bay all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on writing morning times in four digits, adding twelve from one o'clock in the afternoon, the twelve o'clock hours, and changing back.
voiceLines: One day on one line, read two ways. How many hours have passed since midnight?
Read the four digits. Which two are the hours, and which two are the minutes?
Past one in the afternoon, add twelve to the hour. What do you get?
Is twelve noon twelve hours after midnight, or twenty-four? How many whole hours have passed just after midnight?
Is the hour more than twelve? Then take twelve away and write p.m.
A new time. Find it on the line before you write any digits.
Free play. The whole line with both readouts, the gate, the board and the clock bay open.
Slide the marker back to the time, and read both readouts together.
Times written in four digits, noon and the hour after midnight read off the line, and each one changed back.

observations.why: The four digits count from midnight, so a morning hour keeps its number, and four digits name one moment of the day on their own.
observations.soWhat: The 24-hour clock writes four digits, two for the hours and two for the minutes, with no a.m. or p.m.
observations.observe: Each morning time came out in four digits, with a nought in front of a one-digit hour, and none of them carried a.m.

observations.why: By one o'clock in the afternoon the twelve hours before noon have passed and one more, so the count since midnight is thirteen.
observations.soWhat: From one o'clock in the afternoon to just before midnight, twelve is added to the hour.
observations.observe: From one o'clock in the afternoon on, the hour digits read twelve more than the 12-hour hour.

observations.why: Noon is twelve hours after midnight, and just after midnight no whole hour has passed.
observations.soWhat: 12 noon is 1200 hours, and a time just after midnight begins with 00.
observations.observe: On the noon post the digits read 1200 with the gate shut, and just after the left-hand post they began with 00.

observations.why: The take twelve control undoes what the gate added, and the 12-hour row calls the hour just after midnight twelve.
observations.soWhat: To change back, take twelve from an hour of thirteen to twenty-three and write p.m. An hour of 12 keeps its twelve, and 0026 hours is 12:26 a.m.
observations.observe: Each board time found its 12-hour twin: an hour from thirteen on lost twelve and took p.m., an hour of 12 kept its twelve, and 0026 hours became 12:26 a.m.

serves.exercise: finding what a clock that loses two minutes an hour shows five hours after it is set right, in 12-hour and 24-hour time
finding when a film ends from its start and its length, in 24-hour time

source_tool.description: The page's own timeline is drawn large across the working area, a bar numbered nought to twenty-four hours along its top edge. It is shaded one way from midnight to noon and another from noon to midnight. Beneath it the 12-hour times run from 12 midnight through 1 a.m. to 11 a.m., 12 noon, 1 p.m. to 11 p.m., and 12 midnight again. A marker slides along the bar and carries two readouts that move with it: a 12-hour time with a.m. or p.m., and a 24-hour time of four digits and the word hours, the first two digits for the hours and the last two for the minutes. An add twelve gate stands just after the noon post. From one o'clock in the afternoon it adds twelve to the hour, and in the hour from 12 noon to one it stays shut, so that hour keeps its twelve. In the first hour after midnight the hour digits read 00. The right-hand midnight post reads 0000 hours for the start of the next day. A note beside it says the page also writes 2400 hours, a name for midnight at the end of a day. A departure board beside the bar lists times to change either way, and a take twelve control turns a 24-hour hour of thirteen to twenty-three back into a p.m. hour. A clock bay runs a true clock and a clock that gains or loses a few minutes every hour side by side.
source_tool.art_direction: A day's timeline under a departure board / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a clock face with sixty marks, a strip of the day from one midnight to the next, a ladder of units with tiles, the page's own timeline, a column frame, a time track with flags and a hopper, and a wall of month cards.

Every clock is drawn exactly. The minute hand turns six degrees a minute and points exactly at a minute mark, and the hour hand turns thirty degrees an hour and half a degree a minute, so it sits exactly where the time puts it and never on a number except at the hour.

The minute hand is always the longer hand and the hour hand the shorter, and a second hand, where there is one, is the thinnest. A clock face always shows all twelve numbers and all sixty marks, with a longer mark at each number.
A time in figures is written with a colon and a.m. or p.m., as 4:40 p.m., and a 24-hour time as four digits and the word hours, as 1615 hours. Twelve o'clock is written 12 noon or 12 midnight.
Noon and midnight are drawn as posts wherever a strip, a timeline or a track crosses them, and a.m. changes to p.m., or back, only at a post.
A column of time carries at sixty. A carried or broken hour or minute is drawn as sixty cells in six rows of ten, never as ten or as a hundred.
A month card is the real month of the year shown, with its first day under the right weekday and the right number of days, as the calendar in use today lays out that year.
Every day count shows which of its ends it counts. A day that is counted is filled, and a day that is left out is outlined only, at full strength and never hidden.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A hand, a column, a flag or a day is told apart by its shape, its label and its place first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a tile, a cell or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The hour hand, an hour tile, an hours column and the hours of a time split into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand and every minute are deep blue, and the second hand and every second are reddish purple, following the page, whose hour hand is red and whose second hand is a thin pink. The a.m. half of the day, midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on the duration track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile on the ladder are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Every clock rim, minute mark, number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket and guide line is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Slide the marker back to the time, and read both readouts together.
voice.onNext: A new time. Find it on the line before you write any digits.
voice.opening: One day on one line, read two ways. How many hours have passed since midnight?
voice.onFinish: Times written in four digits, noon and the hour after midnight read off the line, and each one changed back.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. The whole line with both readouts, the gate, the board and the clock bay open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Four digits, no a.m. or p.m.

placement.where: After the class has read a printed bus or train timetable in 24-hour time and argued about what a few of its times mean. The tool keeps the four digits and the 12-hour time moving together along one timeline. Noon and the hour after midnight are then read off the line rather than out of a rule.

answer_key.rule: The 24-hour clock counts the hours and minutes since midnight and writes them as four digits and the word hours, with no a.m. or p.m. The first two digits are the hours and the last two the minutes. From 1 a.m. to just before noon the hour keeps its number, written with two digits, so 7:05 a.m. is 0705 hours. From 1 p.m. to just before midnight, twelve is added to the hour, so 9:25 p.m. is 2125 hours. 12 noon is 1200 hours, and a time from noon to just before one keeps its twelve: 12:35 p.m. is 1235 hours. A time from midnight to just before one starts with 00: 12:35 a.m. is 0035 hours. Midnight is 0000 hours at the start of a day, and 2400 hours names the same midnight at the end of a day. To change back, 0000 hours is midnight and 1200 hours is 12 noon. A time with an hour of 00 and minutes past it is twelve and those minutes a.m., and 01 to 11 keep their hour and are a.m. A time with an hour of 12 and minutes past it stays twelve and is p.m., and for hours 13 to 23, take twelve away and write p.m.
answer_key.wrong: The marker is slid back along the timeline to the time, and both readouts are read together while the gate opens or stays shut. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 7:05 a.m. is in the morning, so the hour keeps its number, seven.
The hours take two digits, 07, and the minutes take two digits, 05.
Put them together with no a.m.: 0705 hours.
items.question: Write 7:05 a.m. on the 24-hour clock.
items.checkpoint: The 24-hour clock writes four digits, two for the hours and two for the minutes, with no a.m. or p.m.
items.misconception: Writing 705 hours with only three digits, or dropping the nought in the minutes and writing 075.

steps: 9:25 p.m. is after one o'clock in the afternoon, so twelve is added to the hour.
9 and 12 make 21, and the minutes stay 25.
items.question: Write 9:25 p.m. on the 24-hour clock.
items.checkpoint: From one o'clock in the afternoon to just before midnight, twelve is added to the hour.
items.misconception: Writing 0925 hours, as if p.m. times kept their hour the way a.m. times do.

steps: 12:35 p.m. is thirty-five minutes after noon, and noon is twelve hours after midnight, so it is 1235 hours with nothing added.
12:35 a.m. is thirty-five minutes after midnight, when no whole hour has passed yet.
So its hours are 00, and it is 0035 hours.
items.answer: 12:35 p.m. is 1235 hours, and 12:35 a.m. is 0035 hours
items.question: Write 12:35 p.m. and 12:35 a.m. on the 24-hour clock.
items.checkpoint: 12 noon is 1200 hours, and a time just after midnight begins with 00.
items.misconception: Adding twelve to the twelve and writing 2435 hours for the afternoon time, or writing 1235 hours for the time just after midnight.

steps: In 1650 the hour is 16, which is more than twelve, so take twelve away: 16 less 12 is 4.
The hour was over twelve, so it is p.m.: 4:50 p.m.
In 0340 the hour is 03, less than twelve, so it keeps its number and is a.m.: 3:40 a.m.
items.question: Change 1650 hours and 0340 hours into 12-hour times.
items.checkpoint: To change back, take twelve from an hour of 13 to 23 and write p.m.; hours from 01 to 11 keep their number and are a.m.
items.misconception: Dropping the first digit of 16 and writing 6:50 p.m., instead of taking twelve away.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: What is 0850 hours on the 12-hour clock?
A film starts at 10:40 p.m. Write the time on the 24-hour clock.
Write 12:48 a.m. on the 24-hour clock.
items.final_answer: 0048 hours, because it is forty-eight minutes after midnight

items.question: A child adds twelve to 12 noon, as for the afternoon hours. What does the child write, and what should noon be?
items.final_answer: The child writes 2400 hours, which names midnight at the end of a day. Noon is 1200 hours, twelve hours after midnight, so nothing is added

items.question: Change 0026 hours and 1219 hours into 12-hour times.
A clock gains 3 minutes every hour. It is set right at 9:20 a.m. What does it show 4 hours later? Write the time in 12-hour and in 24-hour time.
items.final_answer: 1:32 p.m., which is 1332 hours. The true time is 1:20 p.m., and the clock has gained 4 times 3, which is 12 minutes

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: runs from nought to twenty-four hours, with the 12-hour times written beneath it
slides along the timeline carrying both readouts
shows the time with a.m. or p.m.
shows the hours and the minutes since midnight, two digits each, and the word hours
adds twelve to the hour from one o'clock in the afternoon, and stays shut in the hour after noon
turns an hour of thirteen to twenty-three back into a p.m. hour

teaching_notes: Read a real timetable in 24-hour time with the class before the tool is opened. The page gives the rule only by example, twelve and one make thirteen and twelve and six make eighteen. It adds twelve only to times from one o'clock in the afternoon on. Its exercise then asks for 12 noon and 12 midnight, and other exercises in the chapter use 12:05 a.m. and 12:15 a.m. A child following the examples adds twelve to noon and writes 2400 hours, a name the page keeps for midnight at the end of a day. So teach what the four digits count, the hours and minutes since midnight, and read the twelve o'clock hours off the timeline. Noon is 1200 hours, and a time just after midnight starts with 00. The page says midnight is 0000 hours and that it can also be written 2400 hours, which names the end of a day. Say that 0000 hours starts a day, and accept either for the exercise that asks for midnight. The page's railway note writes the same times with a colon, 13:45, and this plan writes four digits and the word hours. The box about a slow clock asks for its time in both forms, and the book's key does not answer it: the clock shows 3:00 p.m., which is 1500 hours.
generation_prompt: Build a 24-hour clock tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. The working area holds one long timeline, a bar numbered nought to twenty-four along its top edge, shaded one way from midnight to noon and another from noon to midnight. The 12-hour times are written beneath it from 12 midnight through 11 a.m., 12 noon and 11 p.m. to 12 midnight. A marker slides along the bar in steps of one minute and carries two readouts: a 12-hour time with a.m. or p.m., and a four-digit time with the word hours, split into two hour digits and two minute digits. An add twelve gate after the noon post opens from one o'clock in the afternoon, adding twelve to the hour digits. It stays shut from 12 noon until one, so that hour keeps its twelve. From midnight until one the hour digits read 00. The right-hand post reads 0000 hours for the start of the next day, with a small note that 2400 hours names midnight at the end of a day. A departure board beside the timeline lists times to change either way, and a take twelve control turns an hour of thirteen to twenty-three back into a p.m. hour. A clock bay runs a true clock and a clock that gains or loses a set number of minutes every hour, side by side. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Slide the marker to the time. Read the four digits: hours, then minutes. After one in the afternoon, add twelve. Noon is 1200 hours. Just after midnight starts with 00.
